In a hollow perfectly conducting waveguide of uniform cross-section, a TE mode has fields proportional to exp(i(k z - omega t)) times a transverse profile, and Maxwell's equations in vacuum give omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + omega_c^2, where omega_c is the mode's cutoff frequency fixed by the cross-section geometry and c is the speed of light.
A free relativistic scalar particle of mass m is described by the Klein-Gordon equation, whose plane waves obey omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + (m c^2/hbar)^2.
The two systems are otherwise unrelated: the waveguide relation involves no Planck constant and no particle mass, and its cutoff can be changed by changing the guide dimensions.
omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + omega_c^2

For real D > 0 the fundamental solution of du/dt = D d^2u/dx^2 with u(x,0) = delta(x) is G(x,t) = (4 pi D t)^(-1/2) exp(-x^2/(4 D t)) for t > 0.
The free Schroedinger equation i hbar dpsi/dt = -(hbar^2/2m) d^2psi/dx^2 can be written dpsi/dt = D_q d^2psi/dx^2 with D_q = i hbar/(2m).
The expression for G is continued in D from the positive real axis to D_q along a path in the right half-plane, the square root being taken on the branch that is continuous along this path.
The free-particle propagator is K(x,t) = (m/(2 pi i hbar t))^(1/2) exp(i m x^2/(2 hbar t)).

A stiff string with hinged ends of length L, tension T, linear density mu and bending stiffness EI has partial frequencies f_n given by the dispersion relation omega^2 = (T/mu) k^2 + (EI/mu) k^4 with k_n = n pi/L.
With the inharmonicity parameter B = pi^2 EI/(T L^2) and fundamental f_1 = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu), the partials satisfy f_n = n f_1 (1 + B n^2/2) to first order in the small stiffness parameter B.
A piano bass string has B = 1.0 x 10^-4, and the frequency of its 200th partial is required.
f_200 = 200 f_1 (1 + 2) = 600 f_1

The underdamped oscillator x'' + 2 beta x' + omega0^2 x = 0 with beta < omega0 has solution x(t) = e^{-beta t} [C cos(omega_d t) + D sin(omega_d t)/omega_d], where omega_d = sqrt(omega0^2 - beta^2), C = x(0) and D = x'(0) + beta x(0).
Both cos(omega_d t) and sin(omega_d t)/omega_d are entire functions of omega_d^2, so the solution is an analytic function of the parameter omega_d^2 = omega0^2 - beta^2 and satisfies the differential equation identically in that parameter.
For beta > omega0 define gamma = sqrt(beta^2 - omega0^2), so that omega_d = i gamma.
Continuing the parameter omega_d^2 to negative values gives the overdamped solution x(t) = e^{-beta t} [C cosh(gamma t) + D sinh(gamma t)/gamma] with the same C and D.

An ideal-gas column at rest under uniform gravity satisfies dp/dz = -rho g, with z measured upward.
The column is isothermal at temperature T_0, so p = rho R_s T_0 with constant R_s; consequently rho is a fixed multiple of p at every height, rho = p/(R_s T_0), and rho_0 = p_0/(R_s T_0) at z = 0.
The pressure profile of this column is p(z) = p_0 exp(-g z/(R_s T_0)).
rho(z) = rho_0 exp(-g z/(R_s T_0))

Hydrostatic balance in a fluid at rest, with z measured upward and uniform gravitational acceleration g: dp/dz = -rho g.
The air is an ideal gas, p = rho R_s T, with specific gas constant R_s = 287 J kg^-1 K^-1.
The temperature decreases linearly with height, T(z) = T_0 - Gamma z, with a constant lapse rate Gamma > 0, for 0 <= z < T_0/Gamma; the pressure at z = 0 is p_0.
p(z) = p_0 (1 - Gamma z/T_0)^(g/(R_s Gamma))

In a connected body of liquid at rest, points at the same height have the same pressure, and along any vertical line the pressure increases downward by rho g times the depth.
A U-tube contains water of density rho = 1000 kg m^-3; the free surface in each arm is open to the atmosphere and is treated as a horizontal plane at pressure p_a.
The two arms are cylindrical, one of inner radius 20 mm and the other of inner radius 0.1 mm; h_1 and h_2 denote the heights of the two free surfaces above a common datum.
h_1 = h_2

By the Nyquist-Johnson formula in the engineering convention, the thermal force on a Brownian particle with friction coefficient gamma has one-sided spectral density S_F(f) = 4 gamma k_B T, where f >= 0 is the frequency in Hz and <F^2> = integral_0^infinity S_F(f) df.
A stationary white noise with autocorrelation <F(t) F(t')> = Gamma delta(t - t') has two-sided spectral density S(omega) = integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} <F(t) F(0)> exp(i omega t) dt = Gamma, flat in omega, with <F^2> = integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} S(omega) domega / (2 pi).
For the overdamped Langevin equation gamma dx/dt = F(t) with <F(t) F(t')> = Gamma delta(t - t'), the diffusion coefficient is D = Gamma / (2 gamma^2).
Identifying the flat white-noise spectrum with the Nyquist value gives the diffusion coefficient D = 2 k_B T / gamma.

Dry air obeys the ideal-gas relation p = rho R T, where R is the gas constant for air.
The atmosphere is at rest in uniform gravity g = 9.81 m/s^2 with uniform temperature T = 288 K and obeys dp/dz = -rho g.
The gas constant has the value R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
Eliminating rho gives dp/dz = -g p/(R T), so the pressure decays exponentially with scale height H = R T/g, numerically 244 m.

A driven damped oscillator obeys m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = F0 cos(omega t), and its steady-state motion is x(t) = A cos(omega t - phi) with tan(phi) = b omega / (k - m omega^2), where 0 <= phi <= pi.
The oscillator's angular frequency is omega = sqrt(k/m), so that k - m omega^2 = 0.
phi = pi / 2

The sound intensity level in decibels is defined as L = 10 log10(I/I_0) with reference intensity I_0 = 1.0 x 10^-12 W/m^2.
For a plane sound wave in air of density rho and sound speed c, the intensity is I = p_rms^2/(rho c), where p_rms is the root-mean-square acoustic pressure.
The amplitude of a pure tone is adjusted so that its acoustic pressure amplitude is doubled, all else unchanged.
The sound level rises by Delta L = 10 log10(2) dB, about 3 dB, since the level is ten times the base-ten logarithm of the ratio of the two signals.

Small transverse displacements y(x,t) of a uniform string of tension T and linear density mu obey d^2y/dt^2 = c^2 d^2y/dx^2 with c = sqrt(T/mu), in the rest frame of the string.
This equation is form-invariant under the Lorentz transformation x' = gamma (x - V t), t' = gamma (t - V x/c^2), gamma = 1/sqrt(1 - V^2/c^2), with c = sqrt(T/mu) as the invariant speed, exactly as the electromagnetic wave equation is invariant with the speed of light.
An observer moves along the string at constant speed V < c relative to the string and measures the speed of a transverse pulse.
c' = c

In a medium whose dispersion relation is omega = c k with constant c, every disturbance u(x,t) = f(x - c t) propagates without change of shape at speed c, since d'Alembert's solution applies.
A localized transverse pulse on a long stretched cable resting on a stiff nonlinear foundation is observed to travel several hundred metres at constant speed c_s with no measurable change of shape.
The medium is homogeneous and time-invariant, so it admits a well-defined dispersion relation for small-amplitude sinusoidal waves.
omega = c_s k

The equation of state of air is written in the form p = rho R T, where R is the gas constant.
The gas constant has the value R = 8.314 J mol^-1 K^-1.
The atmosphere is at rest, isothermal at 288 K, under uniform gravity g = 9.81 m s^-2, so that dp/dz = -rho g with z measured upward; combining with the equation of state gives dp/dz = -g p/(R T).
p(z) = p_0 exp(-g z/(R T)), so that the scale height R T/g is about 244 m at 288 K

For an ideal-gas atmosphere with constant lapse rate Gamma > 0, surface temperature T_0 and surface pressure p_0, hydrostatic balance gives p_Gamma(z) = p_0 (1 - Gamma z/T_0)^(g/(R_s Gamma)) for 0 <= z <= T_0/Gamma, and p_Gamma(z) = 0 above the height T_0/Gamma at which the temperature reaches zero.
The isothermal profile is p_iso(z) = p_0 exp(-g z/(R_s T_0)).
For every fixed z >= 0 the limit Gamma -> 0 of p_Gamma(z) is p_iso(z), since (1 - Gamma z/T_0)^(g/(R_s Gamma)) tends to exp(-g z/(R_s T_0)).
p_Gamma(z) = p_iso(z) (1 + O(Gamma)) uniformly in z >= 0, so that for sufficiently small Gamma the isothermal formula reproduces the lapse-rate atmosphere to within any prescribed relative error at all heights

A sinusoidal transverse wave travels along a uniform stretched string of linear mass density mu; its period is T and its wavelength is lambda, so the wave speed is v = lambda / T.
Transverse waves on a string under tension T travel at speed v = sqrt(T/mu), for small-amplitude displacements.
Equating the two expressions for v and solving for lambda gives lambda = T v.
lambda = T^(3/2) / sqrt(mu)

A submarine cable has series resistance r per unit length and shunt capacitance c per unit length; series inductance and shunt leakage conductance are negligible.
Kirchhoff's laws for a line element give dV/dx = -r I and dI/dx = -c dV/dt, where V(x,t) is the voltage to ground and I(x,t) the series current.
The voltage obeys dV/dt = (1/(r c)) d^2V/dx^2, which has the same mathematical form as the one-dimensional heat equation with diffusivity 1/(r c), although V is a potential rather than a conserved density and no random motion of charge carriers is implied.

A particle of mass m moves in one dimension in a smooth potential U(x) with a single minimum at x = 0, where U'(0) = 0 and U''(0) = k > 0.
The particle is released from rest at x = A > 0 and oscillates about x = 0; T denotes the period of this oscillation.
T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k)

In a unidirectional flow of an incompressible Newtonian fluid, momentum diffuses according to du/dt = nu d^2u/dy^2, where nu = eta / rho is the kinematic viscosity with units m^2/s; for water at 20 °C, nu = 1.0e-6 m^2/s.
A dilute passive solute in the same fluid obeys Fick's second law dc/dt = D d^2c/dx^2, where D also has units m^2/s, and a solute molecule's mean squared displacement grows as <x^2> = 2 D t.
Both coefficients are transport coefficients of the same solvent, have the same dimensions m^2/s, and multiply the second spatial derivative in equations of identical form; the water is at rest at 20 °C.
A sucrose molecule in this water therefore has mean squared displacement <x^2> = 2 (1.0e-6 m^2/s) t.

A one-dimensional diffusion process is defined by the Ito stochastic differential equation dx = a(x) dt + b(x) dW, with W a standard Wiener process and a, b smooth; its transition density obeys the Fokker-Planck equation dp/dt = -d(a p)/dx + (1/2) d^2(b^2 p)/dx^2.
A Stratonovich stochastic differential equation dx = A(x) dt + B(x) o dW, defined with the midpoint rule for the stochastic integral, has transition density obeying dp/dt = -d(A p)/dx + (1/2) d/dx [ B d(B p)/dx ].
The two equations are to have the same noise amplitude, B(x) = b(x).
The Ito and Stratonovich equations describe exactly the same stochastic process (identical transition probabilities) if and only if their drifts are related by A(x) = a(x) - (1/2) b(x) b'(x).

A string of linear density mu and tension T attached to an elastic foundation of stiffness s per unit length obeys mu u_tt = T u_xx - s u, i.e. u_tt = c_s^2 u_xx - omega_0^2 u with c_s = sqrt(T/mu) and omega_0 = sqrt(s/mu).
The relativistic Klein-Gordon equation for a free particle of mass m is phi_tt = c^2 phi_xx - (m c^2/hbar)^2 phi, whose plane waves obey E^2 = p^2 c^2 + m^2 c^4 with E = hbar omega and p = hbar k.
The two equations are identical under the replacements c -> c_s and m c^2/hbar -> omega_0, and the quantized string modes carry energy hbar omega and momentum hbar k.
The quanta of transverse waves on the string are therefore relativistic particles of rest mass hbar omega_0 divided by c_s^2, and their energy-momentum relation E^2 = p^2 c_s^2 + m^2 c_s^4 holds in every inertial frame, with c_s playing the role of the invariant speed of special relativity.

Small-amplitude sound in a uniform fluid at rest has acoustic pressure p(x,t) obeying the three-dimensional wave equation p_tt = c^2 nabla^2 p, with c the sound speed.
Attention is restricted to solutions that depend on position only through the distance r from the origin, p = p(r,t), for r > 0.
In spherical coordinates the Laplacian of a function of r alone is (1/r^2) d/dr (r^2 dp/dr), which can be rewritten as (1/r) d^2(r p)/dr^2.
The product r p obeys the one-dimensional wave equation (r p)_tt = c^2 (r p)_rr for r > 0, so spherically symmetric sound consists of outgoing and incoming waves of the form f(r - ct)/r and g(r + ct)/r.

A liquid has a constant isothermal bulk modulus K, so that drho/dp = rho/K, and its density at the surface pressure p_0 is rho_0.
The liquid is at rest under uniform gravity g and obeys dp/dh = rho g, where h is depth below the surface.
The exact solution of these equations is p - p_0 = -K ln(1 - rho_0 g h/K), valid for rho_0 g h < K.
For depths with rho_0 g h << K the gauge pressure is p - p_0 = rho_0 g h, with relative error not exceeding (rho_0 g h/(2K))/(1 - rho_0 g h/K).

An overdamped Brownian particle in a potential U(x) obeys the Langevin equation gamma dx/dt = -U'(x) + xi(t), with gamma the friction coefficient in kg/s and Gaussian white noise <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t').
Its probability density obeys the Smoluchowski equation dp/dt = d/dx[ (U'(x)/gamma) p ] + D d^2p/dx^2 with D = k_B T/gamma.
The potential is now taken to be harmonic, U(x) = (1/2) kappa x^2, with kappa > 0.
The density obeys dp/dt = (kappa/gamma) d(x p)/dx + D d^2p/dx^2.

A random walker on a lattice of spacing a that steps to a random neighbour every tau seconds has, on scales x >> a and t >> tau, a coarse-grained density obeying dc/dt = D d^2c/dx^2 with D = a^2/(2 tau).
In a bench experiment the concentration of a dye in water is found, on millimetre and minute scales, to obey dc/dt = D d^2c/dx^2 with D = 1.0e-9 m^2/s to within measurement error.
The dye molecules therefore move between collisions in steps of a fixed length a separated by a fixed time tau, with a^2 = 2 D tau.

A chain of equal masses m on a line, each joined to its two neighbours by springs of constant K with lattice spacing a, obeys m d^2u_n/dt^2 = K (u_(n+1) - 2 u_n + u_(n-1)) for small displacements u_n, and has travelling-wave solutions u_n = U exp(i(q n a - omega t)) with dispersion relation omega = 2 sqrt(K/m) |sin(q a / 2)|.
A ladder network consists of identical series inductors L between successive nodes, each node connected to ground through a capacitor C, with a nominal cell length a. By Kirchhoff's laws the node charge q_n obeys L d^2q_n/dt^2 = (q_(n+1) - 2 q_n + q_(n-1)) / C, which has the same form as the chain equation under the correspondence m -> L, K -> 1/C, u_n -> q_n.
omega = (2 / sqrt(L C)) |sin(q a / 2)|

The series RLC equation L q'' + R q' + q/C = V(t) and the mechanical equation m x'' + b x' + k x = F(t) are identical in form under q <-> x, L <-> m, R <-> b, 1/C <-> k, V <-> F.
In the mechanical system m is the inertia of the moving body and (1/2) m v^2 is the kinetic energy of that body; correspondingly the inductor's energy (1/2) L I^2 is the energy associated with the moving charge.
The current in the coil's wire, of length l, cross-section A and conduction-electron density n, is I = n e A v_d, carried by N = n A l electrons of mass m_e moving at drift velocity v_d.
Identifying (1/2) L I^2 with the electrons' kinetic energy (1/2) N m_e v_d^2 gives the coil's inductance as L = m_e l/(n e^2 A).

The steady state of m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = F0 cos(omega t) has amplitude A(omega) = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + (2 gamma omega)^2), where omega0 = sqrt(k/m) and gamma = b/(2m).
The damping is weak, gamma << omega0, and the driving frequency lies in the band |omega - omega0| << omega0.
Within this band, with relative error of order |omega - omega0| / omega0, A(omega) = (F0 / (2 m omega0)) / sqrt((omega - omega0)^2 + gamma^2)

The work done on a fluid element in a quasi-static compression is dW = -p dV, and for a liquid of bulk modulus K the compression is reversible and isothermal.
A rigid tank of volume V = 1.0 m^3 is filled with water (K = 2.2e9 Pa) and pumped up to a gauge pressure p = 1.0e7 Pa.
Pressure has the dimensions of energy per unit volume: 1 Pa = 1 J/m^3.
The elastic energy stored in the pressurised water is U = p V, numerically 1.0e7 J.

In a rigid isotropic solid with constant density rho and specific heat c, conservation of energy reads rho c dT/dt = -div q, where q is the heat flux vector.
Every temperature field measured in the solid is found to satisfy the heat equation dT/dt = alpha nabla^2 T with the same constant alpha.
Fourier's law q = -k grad T, inserted into the energy equation, implies the heat equation with alpha = k / (rho c).
Therefore the heat flux in the solid is q = -rho c alpha grad T.

A particle on a one-dimensional lattice of spacing a jumps to each neighbouring site with rate nu/2 (total jump rate nu), the waiting times being exponential and independent.
The occupation probability obeys the master equation dp_n/dt = (nu/2)(p_{n+1} + p_{n-1} - 2 p_n).
The probability is smooth on a length scale L, in the sense that p_n = p(n a, t) with p having bounded derivatives and a << L.
Expanding p(x +/- a) in a Taylor series, the master equation becomes dp/dt = D d^2p/dx^2 with D = nu a^2/2, the neglected term (D a^2/12) d^4p/dx^4 being of relative size O(a^2/L^2).

In an ideal gas of molar mass M and adiabatic index gamma, sound propagates adiabatically with speed c = sqrt(gamma R T/M), where T is the absolute temperature in kelvin and R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
For dry air, gamma and M are taken constant over the range considered, and the speed at T = 273.15 K is c_0 = 331.3 m/s.
The Celsius temperature T_C is defined by T = 273.15 K + T_C, and the regime |T_C| <= 40 is considered.
c = 331.3 m/s + (0.606 m/(s degC)) T_C

A lossless LC circuit stores charge Q on the capacitor and magnetic flux Phi in the inductor. Its Hamiltonian is H = Q^2/(2C) + Phi^2/(2L), with Phi and Q a canonical pair, Poisson bracket {Phi, Q} = 1, so that Hamilton's equations reproduce dPhi/dt = Q/C and dQ/dt = -Phi/L.
The classical oscillation frequency is omega0 = 1/sqrt(LC).
The circuit is quantized by promoting Phi and Q to operators with the Poisson bracket replaced by the commutator [Phi, Q] = i hbar.
The energy spectrum of the quantized circuit is E_n = hbar omega0 (n + 1/2), n = 0, 1, 2, ..., and the classical Hamiltonian is recovered as hbar -> 0.

A resistor R, inductor L and capacitor C are connected in parallel and fed by a current source I_s(t). Kirchhoff's current law for the common node voltage v(t), after one time derivative, is C v'' + (1/R) v' + (1/L) v = I_s'(t).
A driven mechanical oscillator obeys m x'' + b x' + k x = F(t), with quality factor Q = sqrt(k m)/b.
The two equations have identical mathematical form under the correspondence v <-> x, C <-> m, 1/R <-> b, 1/L <-> k, although voltage, capacitance and conductance are not displacement, mass and friction.
Transcribing the mechanical quality factor through this correspondence, the parallel RLC circuit has Q = R sqrt(C/L), the reciprocal of the series-circuit expression, so a larger resistance means lighter damping in the parallel circuit.

A string on an elastic foundation obeys u_tt = c^2 u_xx - omega_0^2 u, with dispersion relation omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + omega_0^2 and group velocity v_g = d omega/dk = c^2 k/omega.
As omega_0 -> 0 the equation reduces to the ordinary wave equation u_tt = c^2 u_xx, for which the group velocity equals c for every wavenumber.
A long-wavelength wave packet is one whose dominant wavenumber satisfies k -> 0.
Long-wavelength packets on the string with foundation travel at the group velocity v_g = c, the foundation being negligible for waves whose spatial scale greatly exceeds any other length in the problem.

A complex scalar field psi(x,t) obeys the Klein-Gordon equation -hbar^2 d^2psi/dt^2 = -hbar^2 c^2 Laplacian psi + m^2 c^4 psi.
The field is written in eikonal form psi = A(x,t) exp(i S(x,t)/hbar) with real A and S, and S is held fixed while hbar -> 0 is taken; terms of order hbar^1 and hbar^2 relative to the leading term are dropped.
S is identified with Hamilton's principal function of a classical particle, so that E = -dS/dt and p = grad S.
(dS/dt)^2 - c^2 (grad S)^2 = m^2 c^4

For m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = F0 cos(omega t) with b > 0, every solution approaches the steady state x_s(t) = A(omega) cos(omega t - phi) as t -> infinity, with A(omega) = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + (b omega/m)^2) and omega0 = sqrt(k/m).
For fixed omega != omega0, as b -> 0 the steady state tends to x_s(t) = F0 cos(omega t) / (m (omega0^2 - omega^2)), since A -> F0/(m |omega0^2 - omega^2|) and phi -> 0 or pi.
Consider the undamped oscillator b = 0 driven at omega != omega0 and starting from rest at x = 0.
lim_(t -> infinity) [ x(t) - F0 cos(omega t) / (m (omega0^2 - omega^2)) ] = 0

A particle on a line moves with constant speed v and reverses direction at the events of a Poisson process of rate lambda (reversals are independent of position and of past history).
Let p_+(x,t) and p_-(x,t) be the probability densities of right-moving and left-moving particles. They obey dp_+/dt + v dp_+/dx = lambda (p_- - p_+) and dp_-/dt - v dp_-/dx = lambda (p_+ - p_-).
The total density is p = p_+ + p_- and the current is j = v (p_+ - p_-).
The total density satisfies the telegraph equation d^2p/dt^2 + 2 lambda dp/dt = v^2 d^2p/dx^2.

For d^2x/dt^2 + 2 gamma dx/dt + omega0^2 x = 0 with 0 < gamma < omega0, the solution with x(0) = A and dx/dt(0) = B - gamma A is x(t) = e^(-gamma t) [ A cos(omega_d t) + B sin(omega_d t) / omega_d ], where omega_d = sqrt(omega0^2 - gamma^2).
Now let gamma > omega0 and define kappa = sqrt(gamma^2 - omega0^2) > 0, so that omega_d is continued to the imaginary value omega_d = i kappa, using cos(i u) = cosh(u) and sin(i u) = i sinh(u).
x(t) = e^(-gamma t) [ A cosh(kappa t) + B sinh(kappa t) / kappa ]

x(t) satisfies d^2x/dt^2 + 2 gamma dx/dt + omega0^2 x = 0, where gamma >= 0 and omega0 > 0 are constants (any ratio gamma/omega0 is allowed).
Define the new dependent variable y(t) = e^(gamma t) x(t), so that x(t) = e^(-gamma t) y(t).
d^2y/dt^2 + (omega0^2 - gamma^2) y = 0

In the hydraulic-electric analogy used for pipe networks, pressure difference corresponds to voltage, volume flow rate Q to current, Poiseuille resistance to Ohmic resistance, and hydraulic power Delta_p Q to electrical power V I.
A hydraulic press consists of two pistons of areas A_1 < A_2 connected by an incompressible fluid at rest with negligible weight; a force F_1 on the small piston balances a force F_2 = F_1 A_2/A_1 on the large one, while a displacement d_1 of the small piston moves the large one by d_2 = d_1 A_1/A_2, so that work is conserved.
An ideal transformer of turns ratio n multiplies voltage by n and divides current by n while conserving power; the press, which multiplies force by A_2/A_1 while conserving work, plays the role of an ideal transformer with n = A_2/A_1 in the hydraulic-electric analogy.
Therefore the pressure at the large piston exceeds that at the small piston by the turns ratio: p_2 = (A_2/A_1) p_1.

Two equal masses m slide without friction on a line. Each mass is joined to a fixed wall by a spring of constant k, and the two masses are joined to each other by a spring of constant kappa. x1 and x2 are the displacements from equilibrium, measured positive in the same direction.
The equations of motion are m d^2x1/dt^2 = -k x1 - kappa (x1 - x2) and m d^2x2/dt^2 = -k x2 - kappa (x2 - x1).
Impose the initial condition x1(0) = A, x2(0) = -A, dx1/dt(0) = dx2/dt(0) = 0.
x1(t) = A cos( sqrt((k + 2 kappa)/m) t )

For a body floating at rest in a liquid of density rho_f, Archimedes' principle gives rho_f g V_sub = M g, where V_sub is the submerged volume and M the mass of the body.
Defining the mean density rho_mean = M/V, with V the total volume of the body, it follows that V_sub/V = rho_mean/rho_f; the submerged fraction therefore determines the mean density of the body.
A log of freshly cut timber floats in fresh water (rho_f = 1000 kg m^-3) with 60 percent of its volume submerged.
rho_substance = 0.60 rho_f, i.e. the solid wood substance (cell-wall material) of which the log is composed has a density of about 600 kg m^-3

A neutrally buoyant particle in a linearly stratified incompressible fluid at rest, with drag and added mass neglected, obeys z'' = -N^2 z, where N^2 = -(g/rho_0) drho/dz > 0.
At time zero the particle is at its equilibrium height and moves upward with speed w_0, so the solution is z(t) = (w_0/N) sin(N t).
Weak stratification corresponds to N -> 0, and in this limit sin(N t)/N -> t.
In a weakly stratified fluid the particle drifts at constant velocity, z(t) = w_0 t, and the stratification may be neglected in computing its position at all later times.

Plane-wave solutions of the Klein-Gordon equation for a particle of mass m > 0 obey omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + (m c^2/hbar)^2, with c the speed of light.
The phase velocity of a plane wave is omega/k, and for these waves omega/k = c sqrt(1 + (m c/(hbar k))^2), which exceeds c for every finite real k.
A signal is any disturbance of the field that propagates through space, and its speed is a velocity measured in metres per second.
v_signal = c sqrt(1 + (m c/(hbar k))^2)

A string of linear density mu under tension T carries the traveling wave u(x,t) = A sin(k x - omega t).
The wave speed is v = omega/k = sqrt(T/mu).
The transverse velocity of a string element is v = du/dt = -A omega cos(k x - omega t), and its magnitude is greatest as the element passes through its equilibrium position.
The maximum transverse speed of a string element is v_max = sqrt(T/mu), reached each time the element crosses the axis.

Hydraulic press: an incompressible liquid at rest connects two pistons of areas A_1 and A_2 at the same level; the pressure under both pistons is the same, and if piston 1 moves down by d_1 the volume conservation A_1 d_1 = A_2 d_2 fixes the displacement d_2 of piston 2.
Law of the lever: a rigid massless bar pivoted at a point with arms l_1 and l_2 is in rotational equilibrium under forces F_1 and F_2 when F_1 l_1 = F_2 l_2; for a small rotation the end displacements satisfy d_1/l_1 = d_2/l_2.
In both systems the work done on one side equals the work delivered on the other, F_1 d_1 = F_2 d_2.
F_2/F_1 = A_2/A_1, in which the area ratio plays the same role that the arm ratio l_1/l_2 plays in the law of the lever

A string of length L, linear density mu and tension T is fixed at both ends; its classical motion is u(x,t) = sum_n q_n(t) sin(n pi x/L) with normal-mode frequencies omega_n = n pi sqrt(T/mu)/L.
Substituting this expansion into the Lagrangian (1/2) integral (mu u_t^2 - T u_x^2) dx gives independent oscillators with effective mass M = mu L/2: L = sum_n (M/2)(q_n'^2 - omega_n^2 q_n^2).
Each mode is quantized canonically by imposing [q_n, p_n] = i hbar with p_n = M q_n', the classical Poisson bracket {q_n, p_n} = 1 being replaced by the commutator.
The allowed energies of mode n are E = hbar omega_n (N + 1/2) with N = 0, 1, 2, ..., and coherent states with N >> 1 reproduce the classical sinusoidal motion of the mode amplitude q_n.

In a connected body of incompressible liquid of density rho at rest under uniform gravity, any two points 1 and 2 satisfy p_1 + rho g z_1 = p_2 + rho g z_2, with z measured upward.
The liquid is enclosed by two frictionless pistons of face areas A_1 and A_2 whose faces are at heights z_1 and z_2; the pressure immediately under piston i equals F_i/A_i, where F_i is the total downward force on that piston (applied load plus piston weight), and the same atmospheric pressure acts on the outside of both pistons so that it cancels.
The two piston faces are held at the same height, z_1 = z_2.
F_2 = F_1 A_2/A_1

A stretched string resting on a uniform elastic foundation (restoring force per unit length -kappa_f y) obeys d^2y/dt^2 = c^2 d^2y/dx^2 - omega_0^2 y with c^2 = T/mu and omega_0^2 = kappa_f/mu, both constant.
For real wavenumber k the dispersion relation is omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + omega_0^2, so propagating solutions exist only for omega >= omega_0.
The string is driven at one end at a fixed angular frequency omega < omega_0, and the steady-state solution y = Y(x) exp(-i omega t) is sought in the form Y = exp(i k x) with k now allowed to be complex, k = i kappa with kappa > 0 chosen so that Y is bounded as x -> +infinity.
kappa = sqrt(omega_0^2 - omega^2)/c

Einstein's 1905 result for a Brownian particle is <Delta x^2(t)> = 2 D t, the mean-square displacement along a single coordinate axis over a time t.
The Stokes-Einstein relation gives D = k_B T/(6 pi eta a) for a sphere of radius a in a fluid of viscosity eta.
In a three-dimensional single-particle tracking experiment the quantity recorded is the full squared displacement |Delta r|^2 = Delta x^2 + Delta y^2 + Delta z^2, averaged over many trajectories.
The recorded mean-square displacement grows as <|Delta r|^2(t)> = k_B T t/(3 pi eta a).

For m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = 0 define omega0 = sqrt(k/m), the quality factor Q = m omega0 / b, and omega_d as the angular frequency of the damped oscillation.
For Q >> 1 the damped frequency is given by omega_d = omega0 (1 - 1/(8 Q^2)), with relative error of order Q^(-4).
Consider the oscillator with b = 2 sqrt(k m), that is Q = 1/2.
omega_d = omega0 / 2

A relativistic field-theory text with metric signature (+,-,-,-) writes the free Klein-Gordon equation as (box + mu^2) phi = 0, where box = d_mu d^mu = (1/c^2) d^2/dt^2 - Laplacian and mu = m c/hbar.
A general-relativity text with metric signature (-,+,+,+) writes the same physical equation as (box - mu^2) phi = 0, where its box is g^{mu nu} d_mu d_nu.
Plane waves phi = exp(i(k.x - omega t)) with real k are substituted into the equation (box - mu^2) phi = 0 using box = (1/c^2) d^2/dt^2 - Laplacian.
omega^2 = c^2 k^2 - (m c^2/hbar)^2

An ideal gas of molar mass M is in hydrostatic balance dp/dz = -rho g with rho = p M/(R T) and g constant.
The temperature falls linearly with height, T(z) = T_0 - L z, with constant lapse rate L > 0, so that the exact pressure profile is p(z) = p_0 (1 - L z/T_0)^(g M/(R L)).
Only altitudes satisfying L z/T_0 << 1 are considered.
In this regime the pressure is approximated by the isothermal form p(z) = p_0 exp(-M g z/(R T_0)), with the relative error in ln(p/p_0) not exceeding (L z/(2 T_0))/(1 - L z/T_0).

A simple pendulum obeys theta'' + omega0^2 sin(theta) = 0 with omega0^2 = g/L; it is released from rest at angle theta0.
For small angles sin(theta) = theta - theta^3/6 + ..., so the exact equation differs from the linearized equation theta'' + omega0^2 theta = 0 by terms of order theta0^3.
The linearized equation with the same initial conditions has the solution theta0 cos(omega0 t).
Hence for small release angles the exact motion is theta(t) = theta0 cos(omega0 t) + O(theta0^3), the error bound holding uniformly for all t >= 0.

The free-particle Schrodinger equation i hbar dpsi/dt = -(hbar^2 / 2m) d^2psi/dx^2 can be rewritten as dpsi/dt = D_q d^2psi/dx^2 with the imaginary coefficient D_q = i hbar / (2m).
A diffusion equation dp/dt = D d^2p/dx^2 with real D > 0 describes a random walker whose mean squared displacement grows as <x^2> = 2 D t.
For the quantum particle the position variance is computed from |psi|^2, and the initial state is a real Gaussian wavepacket of width sigma_0 centred at x = 0.
Because the Schrodinger equation is a diffusion equation with diffusion constant of magnitude hbar / (2m), the wavepacket spreads diffusively as <x^2>(t) = hbar t / m.

A Brownian sphere of radius a in a fluid of viscosity eta is described by the overdamped Langevin equation 6 pi eta a dx/dt = xi(t) with <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 (6 pi eta a) k_B T delta(t - t'), which gives <Delta x^2(t)> = 2 D t with D = k_B T/(6 pi eta a) for all t > 0.
A silica bead has a = 0.5e-6 m and density 2000 kg/m^3; it is suspended in water with eta = 1.0e-3 Pa s at T = 300 K, so D = 4.4e-13 m^2/s.
The bead's position is sampled with a time resolution of 1 ns.
Over one sampling interval the mean-square displacement along x is <Delta x^2(1 ns)> = 2 D t = 8.8e-22 m^2.

A quantum particle of mass m in a potential U(x), coupled to an Ohmic bath at temperature T with k_B T >> hbar gamma, has a Wigner function obeying the Caldeira-Leggett master equation dW/dt = -(p/m) dW/dx + U'(x) dW/dp - (hbar^2/24) U'''(x) d^3W/dp^3 + O(hbar^4) + gamma d(p W)/dp + gamma m k_B T d^2W/dp^2, where gamma is the momentum damping rate in 1/s.
The classical limit is taken as hbar -> 0 with m, T, gamma and U fixed, the Wigner function remaining smooth in p on scales set by m k_B T.
In this limit W obeys the classical Kramers equation dW/dt = -(p/m) dW/dx + U'(x) dW/dp + gamma d(p W)/dp + gamma m k_B T d^2W/dp^2.

A series RLC circuit with L = 1.0 mH, C = 1.0 microfarad and R = 60 ohm is driven by an ideal source V0 cos(omega t). Writing omega0^2 = 1/(LC), the steady-state charge amplitude is q0 = (V0/L) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + (R omega/L)^2).
The capacitor voltage amplitude is V_C = q0/C, so V_C(omega) = V0 omega0^2 / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + (R omega/L)^2).
Setting the derivative of the expression under the square root with respect to omega^2 to zero locates the extremum of V_C.
The capacitor voltage is therefore maximal at a driving frequency somewhat below resonance, omega_max^2 = 1/(LC) - R^2/(2 L^2).

A uniform string of linear density mu under tension T undergoes small transverse displacements u(x,t) obeying mu u_tt = T u_xx.
The kinetic energy per unit length is (1/2) mu u_t^2 and the potential energy per unit length, from the extra stretching of the string, is (1/2) T u_x^2.
The string carries a sinusoidal wave of wavenumber k and angular frequency omega = k sqrt(T/mu).
At every point and every instant the two energy densities are equal, (1/2) mu u_t^2 = (1/2) T u_x^2, so the kinetic and potential energies of the wave are always identical.

A function u(x,t) is twice continuously differentiable and satisfies the one-dimensional wave equation d^2u/dt^2 = c^2 d^2u/dx^2 with constant c > 0 on the whole real line.
New independent variables are introduced by xi = x - c t and eta = x + c t; this map is linear and invertible with x = (xi + eta)/2 and t = (eta - xi)/(2c).
Derivatives transform by the chain rule: d/dx = d/dxi + d/deta and d/dt = -c d/dxi + c d/deta.
d^2u/(dxi deta) = 0

The free damped oscillator d^2x/dt^2 + 2 gamma dx/dt + omega0^2 x = 0 with 0 < gamma < omega0 has solutions whose amplitude decays as exp(-gamma t), and the energy E is proportional to the square of the amplitude.
For a lightly damped oscillator the quality factor is Q = omega0 / gamma, where gamma is the damping constant of the oscillator.
E0 denotes the energy at t = 0.
E(t) = E0 exp(-2 omega0 t / Q)

An incompressible fluid at rest under uniform gravity g has an unknown smooth density profile rho(z), and its pressure obeys dp/dz = -rho(z) g.
Integrating the pressure over the surface of any fully submerged body gives the buoyant force F_b = g times the integral of rho over the displaced volume (Archimedes' principle for a stratified fluid).
A rigid sphere of radius a and volume V is held fully submerged with its centre at height z_c, and the net force exerted by the fluid on it, F_b(z_c), is measured as z_c is varied.
Since the buoyant force is determined by the density profile, the measurement determines the density profile: rho(z) = F_b(z)/(g V) at every height z.

A beaded string consists of point masses m at spacing a on a massless string under tension T; the transverse displacement y_n of bead n obeys m y_n'' = (T/a)(y_(n+1) - 2 y_n + y_(n-1)) for small displacements.
The exact normal modes are y_n = A exp(i(k n a - omega t)) with omega = 2 sqrt(T/(m a)) |sin(k a/2)|.
One considers only motions that vary slowly on the scale of the bead spacing, k a << 1, and describes them by a smooth field u(x,t) with u(n a, t) = y_n(t) and mass per unit length mu equal to m/a.
The slowly varying field obeys the continuum string equation mu u_tt = T u_xx, whose dispersion omega = sqrt(T/mu) k reproduces the beaded-string result to leading order in k a.

A connected region of fluid at rest obeys the hydrostatic equation grad p = rho g_vec, where g_vec is the gravitational field and rho the local density.
Consider the special case in which the gravitational body force is absent or negligible, g_vec = 0 (for example a small hydraulic device in which rho g times the height differences is negligible compared with the applied pressures).
A pressure p_a is applied at one part of the boundary of the fluid.
Throughout the connected fluid region p = p_a, so the applied pressure is transmitted undiminished to every point and every wall.

An ideal LC circuit (no resistance) has energy H = q^2/(2C) + Phi^2/(2L), where q is the capacitor charge and Phi = L I is the flux linkage of the inductor; Hamilton's equations with q as coordinate and Phi as conjugate momentum reproduce dq/dt = I and L dI/dt = -q/C.
The circuit is quantized canonically by promoting q and Phi to operators with [q, Phi] = i hbar, and E_n (n = 0, 1, 2, ...) denote the energy eigenvalues of the resulting Hamiltonian.
E_n = hbar (n + 1/2) / sqrt(L C)

A string of linear density mu and tension T is attached along its length to an elastic foundation of stiffness s per unit length, so that small transverse motion obeys u_tt = c^2 u_xx - omega_0^2 u with c = sqrt(T/mu) and omega_0 = sqrt(s/mu).
For propagating waves exp(i(k x - omega t)) the dispersion relation is k^2 = (omega^2 - omega_0^2)/c^2, which requires omega > omega_0 for real k.
The string occupying x > 0 is driven at x = 0 at a frequency omega below omega_0, and only solutions bounded as x -> infinity are admitted.
Continuing the wavenumber to the imaginary value k = i kappa gives the bounded steady-state solution u = A exp(-kappa x) cos(omega t) with kappa = sqrt(omega_0^2 - omega^2)/c.

A twice continuously differentiable field u(x,t) on the whole line satisfies the one-dimensional wave equation u_tt = c^2 u_xx with constant c > 0.
Define the characteristic (Riemann) variables r = u_t + c u_x and s = u_t - c u_x.
The wave equation is equivalent to a pair of decoupled first-order advection equations for r and s, the right-moving one being r_t - c r_x = 0, while s obeys the mirror equation with c replaced by -c; conversely, from any smooth (r, s) obeying these two equations one recovers a solution u of the wave equation, unique up to a constant.

A string on an elastic foundation obeys u_tt = c^2 u_xx - omega_0^2 u, so propagating waves exp(i(k x - omega t)) exist only for omega > omega_0, with wavenumber k = 2 pi/lambda.
When the string occupying x > 0 is driven at x = 0 at a frequency omega < omega_0, the bounded solution is u = A exp(-kappa x) cos(omega t) with kappa = sqrt(omega_0^2 - omega^2)/c.
The constant kappa is measured in inverse metres, exactly like the wavenumber k of a propagating wave.
Below cutoff the disturbance therefore has wavelength lambda = 2 pi/kappa, which shrinks toward zero as the drive frequency is lowered far below omega_0.

A massless string under tension T carries point masses m at equal spacing a; the transverse displacement y_j of mass j obeys m d^2y_j/dt^2 = (T/a)(y_{j+1} - 2 y_j + y_{j-1}) for small displacements.
Normal modes y_j = exp(i(k j a - omega t)) have the exact dispersion relation omega = 2 sqrt(T/(m a)) |sin(k a/2)|.
Only disturbances whose wavelength is much larger than the spacing, k a << 1, are considered, and a smooth field y(x,t) is defined so that y(j a, t) = y_j(t) with mu = m/a the average mass per unit length.
d^2y/dt^2 = (T a/m) d^2y/dx^2

Transverse waves on a uniform string of linear density mu obey mu u_tt = T u_xx, obtained from Newton's second law by taking the tension along the string to be uniform and equal to the static tension T and linearizing in the slope u_x.
Traveling-wave solutions of this equation move at sqrt(T/mu), independent of amplitude and wavelength.
A string with T = 50 N and mu = 5.0 x 10^-3 kg/m carries a sinusoidal wave of wavelength 5.0 cm and amplitude 3.0 cm.
The crests of this wave advance along the string at v = 100 m/s, the value of sqrt(T/mu).

In a liquid of density rho_f at rest under gravity g, the pressure at depth d below the free surface is p = p_atm + rho_f g d.
The force exerted by the liquid on a surface element dA of a body, with unit normal n pointing out of the body, is -p n dA.
A rectangular block of base area A, height b and volume V = A b rests on the flat horizontal bottom of a tank filled with the liquid to depth H > b.
Summing the vertical pressure forces on the top and bottom faces, the liquid exerts a net upward force on the block equal to F = rho_f g V.

When a flat plate bounding a fluid at rest is impulsively set in motion, the fluid velocity obeys du/dt = nu d^2u/dy^2 with nu = eta/rho, and vorticity has penetrated a distance delta_v(t) = 2 (nu t)^(1/2) after time t.
When the same plate is instead suddenly heated, the fluid temperature obeys dT/dt = alpha d^2T/dy^2 with alpha = k/(rho c_p).
Both nu and alpha are diffusivities measured in m^2/s, and the two governing equations are identical in form.
The thermal penetration depth therefore equals the viscous one, delta_T(t) = 2 (nu t)^(1/2).

The Goldstein-Kac density obeys d^2p/dt^2 + 2 lambda dp/dt = v^2 d^2p/dx^2 with p(x,0) = delta(x) and dp/dt(x,0) = 0.
In the diffusion limit lambda -> infinity, v -> infinity with D = v^2/(2 lambda) fixed, p(x,t) converges for each fixed x and t to G(x,t) = (4 pi D t)^(-1/2) exp(-x^2/(4 D t)).
For finite but large lambda the diffusion limit is approached once t >> 1/lambda.
For t >> 1/lambda the telegraph solution is described by the Gaussian throughout space, p(x,t) = G(x,t) (1 + O(1/(lambda t))) for all x.

A Brownian particle of mass m and friction coefficient gamma obeys m dv/dt = -gamma v + xi(t) with <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t'), in equilibrium at temperature T.
In the limit m -> 0 at fixed gamma and T, the position process converges to the overdamped Langevin equation gamma dx/dt = xi(t), whose mean squared displacement is <(Delta x)^2> = 2 D t with D = k_B T / gamma for every t > 0.
For a micrometre-sized colloidal sphere in water the momentum relaxation time m / gamma is a few hundred nanoseconds, so m is negligibly small and the overdamped description is taken to apply.
Hence the mean squared displacement of the colloidal sphere is linear at all times, with initial slope d<(Delta x)^2>/dt at t = 0 equal to 2 k_B T / gamma.

A mass m hangs from a linear spring of constant k in a uniform gravitational field g. The coordinate x is the extension of the spring beyond its unstretched length, positive downward, so Newton's law reads m x'' = -k x + m g.
Define the new coordinate y = x - m g/k, the displacement measured from the static equilibrium position.
In the variable y the motion obeys y'' = -(k/m) y, so the hanging spring in gravity and the free horizontal mass-spring oscillator are the same oscillator; gravity only shifts the centre of oscillation and leaves the frequency unchanged.

A particle in one dimension moves at constant speed v and reverses its direction at random instants forming a Poisson process; the mean time between successive reversals is tau.
The probability density of such a persistent random walk obeys the telegraph equation tau d^2p/dt^2 + dp/dt = D d^2p/dx^2, where tau is the relaxation time of the velocity autocorrelation <v(0) v(t)> = v^2 exp(-t / tau) and D = v^2 tau is the long-time diffusion coefficient (partial derivatives understood).
The long-time diffusion coefficient of the persistent random walk is D = v^2 tau, where tau is the mean time between reversals.

A solute of molecular diffusivity D is carried by steady laminar Poiseuille flow u(r) = 2U(1 - r^2/a^2) in a straight circular tube of radius a, U being the cross-sectionally averaged speed.
The concentration obeys dc/dt + u(r) dc/dz = D ( (1/r) d/dr (r dc/dr) + d^2c/dz^2 ) with zero radial flux at the wall r = a.
Times considered satisfy t >> a^2/D, so the solute has sampled the whole cross-section many times, and the cross-sectionally averaged concentration C(z,t) = (2/a^2) integral_0^a c r dr varies slowly along z.
The averaged concentration obeys the one-dimensional advection-diffusion equation dC/dt + U dC/dz = D_eff d^2C/dz^2 with D_eff = D + a^2 U^2/(48 D).

Two identical pendulums (mass m, omega0 = sqrt(g/l)) coupled by a weak spring of constant kappa, with pendulum 1 initially excited, exchange energy so that the fraction in pendulum 2 averaged over the fast oscillation is E2/E0 = sin^2(Delta t / 2), where Delta = omega_- - omega_+ = kappa / (m omega0) to first order in kappa/(m omega0^2).
A two-level atom initially in its ground state and driven resonantly by a classical field has excited-state probability P_e(t) = sin^2(Omega_R t / 2), where Omega_R is the Rabi frequency (optical Bloch equations in the rotating-wave approximation).
Both systems are governed by the same pair of coupled first-order equations for two slowly varying amplitudes, so the coupled pendulums are a two-level quantum system whose Rabi frequency is set by the spring coupling.
Omega_R = kappa / (m omega0)

A stiff string of linear density mu, tension T, Young's modulus E and area moment I undergoes small transverse motion obeying mu u_tt = T u_xx - E I u_xxxx (Euler-Bernoulli bending term added to the ideal-string equation).
Sinusoidal waves exp(i(kx - omega t)) therefore satisfy the exact dispersion relation omega^2 = (T/mu) k^2 + (E I/mu) k^4; write c = sqrt(T/mu) and epsilon = E I k^2 / T.
The regime considered is epsilon << 1, i.e. wavelengths long compared with sqrt(E I / T).
In this regime omega = c k (1 + E I k^2 /(2 T)), with relative error no larger than about epsilon^2/8, so the wave is slightly dispersive with phase speed increasing quadratically with k.

A particle moving in one dimension has a stationary velocity process v(t) with autocorrelation C(t) = <v(0) v(t)>, satisfying C(-t) = C(t), and C decays fast enough that integral_0^infinity |C(t)| dt and integral_0^infinity t |C(t)| dt are both finite.
The displacement is x(t) - x(0) = integral_0^t v(t') dt', so that, by stationarity, <(x(t) - x(0))^2> = 2 integral_0^t (t - s) C(s) ds.
The diffusion coefficient is defined as D = lim_{t -> infinity} <(x(t) - x(0))^2> / (2 t).
D = integral_0^infinity C(t) dt.

A tank contains water of density rho at rest under uniform gravity; the pressure at depth d below the free surface is p(d) = p_a + rho g d.
A rectangular block of height c and horizontal cross-section a x b, volume V = a b c, lies flat on the horizontal floor of the tank with its top face at depth D.
The top face and the four vertical faces of the block are in contact with the water; the force exerted by the water on the block is the sum of the pressure forces on its faces, each normal to the face and directed into the block.
Pressure forces on opposite vertical faces cancel because the pressure distribution is the same on both.
F = rho g V, directed upward

Fourier's law q = -k dT/dx relates the heat flux in a solid to the temperature gradient through the thermal conductivity k; combined with steady-state energy conservation dq/dx = 0 it gives a linear temperature profile across a slab.
A single-crystal silicon film of thickness L = 20 nm at 300 K is held between two reservoirs differing in temperature by Delta T. The bulk thermal conductivity of silicon at 300 K is k = 150 W/(m K), and the phonons carrying most of the heat at this temperature have mean free paths of order 300 nm.
Transport across the film is one-dimensional and steady.
The steady heat flux through the film is q = (150 W/(m K)) Delta T / L.

A mass m on a linear spring of constant k, with a viscous damping force -b x', is driven by F0 cos(omega t). The equation of motion is written x'' + 2 beta x' + omega0^2 x = (F0/m) cos(omega t), with beta = b/(2m) and omega0^2 = k/m.
After the transients have decayed, the displacement is x = A cos(omega t - delta) with A = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4 beta^2 omega^2).
The damping is light enough that 2 beta^2 < omega0^2.
The steady-state amplitude A is largest at the driving frequency omega_r given by omega_r^2 = omega0^2 - 2 beta^2, which lies below the natural frequency omega0.

An incompressible Newtonian fluid of kinematic viscosity nu fills the half-space y > 0 above a flat plate; at t = 0 the plate is impulsively set moving in its own plane at speed U_0. With no pressure gradient and a unidirectional velocity u = u(y, t), the Navier-Stokes equations reduce to du/dt = nu d^2u/dy^2 with u(0, t) = U_0, u(y, 0) = 0 and u -> 0 as y -> infinity.
A semi-infinite solid y > 0 of thermal diffusivity alpha, initially at uniform temperature T_i, has its surface held at T_s for t > 0. Its temperature obeys dT/dt = alpha d^2T/dy^2 and is given by (T - T_i) / (T_s - T_i) = erfc( y / (2 sqrt(alpha t)) ).
The velocity profile has the same mathematical form as the temperature profile, with the kinematic viscosity in the role of the thermal diffusivity: u(y, t) / U_0 = erfc( y / (2 sqrt(nu t)) ).

An ideal gas of spin-1/2 fermions of mass m is held at temperature T in uniform gravity g along -z; in the local-density approximation (valid when the thermal de Broglie wavelength lambda_T = h/sqrt(2 pi m k_B T) is small compared with k_B T/(m g)) the number density is n(z) = -(2/lambda_T^3) Li_{3/2}(-zeta exp(-m g z/(k_B T))), where zeta is the fugacity and Li_{3/2} the polylogarithm.
The classical (non-degenerate) limit is zeta -> 0, equivalently n lambda_T^3 -> 0, which is the limit h -> 0 at fixed n and T; in this limit Li_{3/2}(-x) = -x + O(x^2).
n(z) = n(0) exp(-m g z/(k_B T))

Two uniform strings of linear densities mu_1 (x < 0) and mu_2 (x > 0) are joined at x = 0 by a massless knot and carry the same static tension T; small transverse displacements obey mu_i u_tt = T u_xx on each side.
A sinusoidal wave of angular frequency omega is incident from x < 0; the displacement u and the slope u_x are continuous at x = 0 (the knot has no mass, so the transverse forces on it balance).
The characteristic impedance of each string is defined as Z_i = sqrt(T mu_i), so that the wavenumbers are k_i = omega Z_i / T.
The amplitude reflection coefficient for the displacement, referred to the incident amplitude, is r = (Z_1 - Z_2)/(Z_1 + Z_2).

Two bodies slide without friction along a line. Each is attached to a fixed wall by a linear spring of constant k, and the two bodies are joined to each other by a linear spring of constant kappa. Let m denote the mass of the first body, and consider small oscillations.
The normal modes are the in-phase motion, in which both bodies move together and the coupling spring stays at its natural length, and the anti-phase motion, in which the midpoint of the coupling spring stays at rest and each body feels an extra restoring force 2 kappa times its displacement.
The anti-phase normal mode has angular frequency given by omega_2^2 = (k + 2 kappa)/m.

Solid spheres of density rho_p and volume V_p are uniformly dispersed at volume fraction phi in a liquid of density rho_f in a vessel; the mean interparticle spacing is very small compared with the depth h of the suspension.
Each sphere falls at its terminal velocity, so the hydrodynamic force exerted on it by the liquid is upward and equal to (rho_p - rho_f) g V_p; by Newton's third law the sphere exerts an equal and opposite force on the liquid.
On the microscopic scale the liquid pressure varies around each particle; the pressure p(h) is defined as the average of the liquid pressure over horizontal slabs whose thickness is large compared with the interparticle spacing but small compared with h.
For such a slab, vertical force balance includes the weight of the liquid in the slab and the forces transmitted to the liquid by the particles within it; the pressure at the free surface is p_0.
p(h) = p_0 + [phi rho_p + (1 - phi) rho_f] g h

A liquid of uniform density rho fills an open cylindrical bucket that rotates about its vertical axis with constant angular velocity omega; in the co-rotating frame the liquid is at rest.
In the co-rotating frame the body force per unit volume is rho(-g e_z + omega^2 r e_r), where r is the distance from the axis and z is measured upward, and the liquid obeys the hydrostatic balance grad p = rho(-g e_z + omega^2 r e_r).
The free surface is the isobar on which p equals the atmospheric pressure p_atm, and it meets the axis at height z_0.
The free surface is the paraboloid z(r) = z_0 + omega^2 r^2/(2 g).

A diver's pressure gauge is calibrated to read zero at the free surface; at depth h in water of density rho = 1000 kg m^-3 it reads p_gauge = rho g h with g = 9.81 m s^-2, i.e. 1.0 x 10^5 Pa per 10.2 m of depth.
A small air bubble is released at a depth of 20.4 m, where the gauge reads 2.0 x 10^5 Pa, and rises to a depth of 10.2 m, where the gauge reads 1.0 x 10^5 Pa; water and bubble are at the same uniform temperature throughout.
The air in the bubble obeys Boyle's law at constant temperature, p V = constant, and the pressure inside the bubble equals the water pressure at its position (surface tension neglected).
V_2/V_1 = 2

A particle of mass m obeys the Langevin equation m dv/dt = -gamma v + xi(t), where gamma > 0 is a friction coefficient with units kg/s.
xi(t) is Gaussian white noise with <xi(t)> = 0 and <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t').
At t = 0 the velocity is in thermal equilibrium, <v(0)^2> = k_B T / m, and v(0) is uncorrelated with xi(t) for all t > 0 (causality).
<v(0) v(t)> = (k_B T / m) exp(-gamma t / m) for t >= 0.

For the weakly damped oscillator m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = 0 with b << sqrt(k m), the energy E = (1/2) m (dx/dt)^2 + (1/2) k x^2 averaged over one cycle, <E>, obeys d<E>/dt = -(b/m) <E>, so that <E>(t) = E0 exp(-b t/m).
Because the cycle average commutes with d/dt and the exponential law for <E> holds at every instant t, the same first-order law governs the unaveraged energy E(t).
dE/dt = -(b/m) E

An ideal gas of molar mass M with temperature profile T(z) is in hydrostatic balance dp/dz = -rho g with rho = p M/(R T) and g constant; p > 0 everywhere.
Because dp/dz < 0, p(z) is strictly decreasing, so height can be used as a function of pressure, z = z(p).
The geopotential is defined as Phi = g z.
In pressure coordinates the hydrostatic equation reads dPhi/d(ln p) = -R T/M, and this hypsometric form and the height-coordinate form dp/dz = -rho g imply each other.

For a lightly damped oscillator written in the form x'' + gamma x' + omega0^2 x = 0, the stored energy decays as e^{-gamma t} and the quality factor is defined by Q = omega0/gamma.
The series RLC circuit obeys L q'' + R q' + q/C = 0 with omega0^2 = 1/(LC); its charge amplitude decays as e^{-R t/(2L)}, so the circuit's damping rate is gamma = R/(2L).
The circuit equation has the same form as the mechanical one, so the mechanical definition of Q may be carried over term by term.
The quality factor of the series RLC circuit is Q = 2 omega0 L / R.

An ideal gas of molar mass M = 0.02896 kg/mol is in hydrostatic balance dp/dz = -rho g with rho = p M/(R T), g = 9.81 m/s^2 and R = 8.314 J/(mol K).
Near the ground the temperature falls linearly with height at the tropospheric lapse rate L = 6.5e-3 K/m from T_0 = 288 K, and the surface pressure is p_0 = 101325 Pa.
Integrating the hydrostatic equation with this temperature profile gives p(z) = p_0 (1 - L z/T_0)^(g M/(R L)).
Evaluating this expression at an altitude of 40 km gives p(40 km) = 0.5 Pa.

An overdamped Brownian particle in one dimension obeys the Smoluchowski equation dp/dt = d/dx [ D0 ( dp/dx + (V'(x) / (k_B T)) p ) ] with a constant bare diffusivity D0 (partial derivatives understood).
The potential V(x) is smooth and periodic with period L, V(x + L) = V(x), and the bath is at temperature T.
Angle brackets <f> denote the spatial average (1/L) integral_0^L f(x) dx over one period.
On length scales much larger than L and times much longer than L^2 / D0, the particle performs ordinary diffusion with effective coefficient D_eff = D0 / ( <exp(V / k_B T)> <exp(-V / k_B T)> ).

A passive scalar u(x,t) in a uniform flow of velocity v along x obeys the advection-diffusion equation du/dt + v du/dx = D d^2u/dx^2 on the whole real line, with D a constant.
Define the co-moving coordinate xi = x - v t and the function w(xi,t) = u(xi + v t, t).
u solves the advection-diffusion equation if and only if w solves the pure diffusion equation dw/dt = D d^2w/dxi^2.

A liquid has density depending linearly on pressure, rho = rho_0 [1 + kappa (p - p_0)], with constant compressibility kappa (for water about 4.6 x 10^-10 Pa^-1) and density rho_0 at the surface pressure p_0.
With depth h measured downward from the free surface, hydrostatic balance reads dp/dh = rho g with g uniform.
The exact solution of this system is p(h) - p_0 = (1/kappa) [exp(kappa rho_0 g h) - 1].
The regime considered is kappa rho_0 g h << 1 (for water this parameter is about 0.045 at h = 10 km).
p(h) = p_0 + rho_0 g h (1 + kappa rho_0 g h/2), with relative error in the pressure excess of order (kappa rho_0 g h)^2/6

A uniform stiff string of linear mass density mu, tension T and bending stiffness EI (Young's modulus times second moment of area) has small transverse displacement y(x,t) obeying mu d^2y/dt^2 = T d^2y/dx^2 - EI d^4y/dx^4, valid for wavelengths long compared with the string's thickness.
For plane waves y = exp(i(kx - omega t)) with real k this gives the dispersion relation omega^2 = (T/mu) k^2 + (EI/mu) k^4.
The tension is now set to zero, T = 0, all other parameters being unchanged.
omega = sqrt(EI/mu) k^2

An ideal gas of molecules of mass m is in thermal equilibrium at uniform temperature T in a uniform gravitational field g, with the z axis pointing upward.
The single-particle equilibrium distribution is the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution f(r, v) proportional to exp(-(m v^2/2 + m g z)/(k_B T)).
The continuum pressure is defined as the z-momentum flux p = integral of m v_z^2 f d^3v, averaged over a volume that contains many molecules but is small compared with the height k_B T/(m g).
The averaged pressure field is p(z) = p_0 exp(-m g z/(k_B T)), which satisfies the hydrostatic equation dp/dz = -rho g with rho the averaged mass density.

A lossless transmission line with inductance L' and capacitance C' per unit length obeys the telegrapher's equations V_x = -L' I_t and I_x = -C' V_t, so that V_tt = (1/(L' C')) V_xx.
A uniform string of linear density mu under tension T obeys u_tt = (T/mu) u_xx; its transverse force F = -T u_x and transverse velocity u_t satisfy F_x = -mu (u_t)_t and (u_t)_x = -(1/T) F_t.
The two systems are described by the same pair of first-order equations under V <-> F, I <-> u_t, L' <-> mu, C' <-> 1/T, so the line's signal speed v = 1/sqrt(L' C') plays the role of the string's sqrt(T/mu) and sqrt(L'/C') plays the role of the string impedance sqrt(T mu), even though one system carries voltages and currents and the other displacements and forces.

A mass m on a spring of constant k with viscous damping -b x' is driven sinusoidally. In the steady state x = A cos(omega t - delta), and the average power dissipated by the damping force over one cycle is P = (1/2) b omega^2 A^2, where omega is the angular frequency appearing in x(t).
The oscillator's angular frequency satisfies omega^2 = k/m.
Substituting the second relation into the first, the average dissipated power is P = b k A^2/(2 m), whatever the frequency at which the oscillator is driven.

An isothermal ideal-gas atmosphere in uniform gravity has pressure p(z) = p_0 exp(-z/H) with scale height H = R T/(M g), obtained from dp/dz = -p/H.
Monochromatic light travelling a distance x through a homogeneous absorber obeys the Beer-Lambert law I(x) = I_0 exp(-x/l), obtained from dI/dx = -I/l with absorption length l.
The two laws are solutions of the same first-order equation dy/ds = -y/lambda, and under the correspondence z <-> x, H <-> l one profile maps onto the other: p(z)/p_0 = I(z l/H)/I_0.

In water at rest under uniform gravity the pressure at depth h is p(h) = p_a + rho g h, where rho g h is the pressure excess over atmospheric produced by the weight of the overlying water.
The pascal is identical to the joule per cubic metre, so pressure has the dimensions of an energy per unit volume.
Water at depth is slightly compressed by the pressure and therefore stores elastic energy in its compressed state.
u(h) = rho g h, where u is the elastic energy stored per unit volume of water at depth h

Two identical pendulums (bob mass m, length l, omega0 = sqrt(g/l)) swing at small angles in the same plane; their bobs are joined by a weak spring of constant kappa with kappa/(m omega0^2) << 1.
The normal modes are the in-phase mode with angular frequency omega_+ = omega0 and the anti-phase mode with omega_- = sqrt(omega0^2 + 2 kappa/m); define Delta = omega_- - omega_+.
At t = 0 pendulum 1 is released from rest with displacement A and pendulum 2 is at rest at its equilibrium position.
E1(t) denotes the kinetic plus gravitational potential energy of pendulum 1 averaged over one period 2 pi/omega0 of the fast oscillation, and E0 = (1/2) m omega0^2 A^2 is the initial energy.
E1(t) = E0 cos^2(Delta t / 2)

Dry sand of bulk density rho_b = 1600 kg m^-3 fills a tall vertical cylindrical silo of diameter 3 m to a height h and is at rest.
Like a liquid, the sand has no shape of its own, conforms to the container, and transmits contact forces between neighbouring grains; the granular column is therefore treated as a liquid of density rho_b at rest under gravity.
For a liquid at rest, vertical force balance on a thin horizontal slab of thickness dh gives dp/dh = rho g with p = 0 (gauge) at the free surface; the same slab balance is applied to the granular column with the vertical compressive stress sigma across horizontal planes in place of p.
sigma(h) = rho_b g h

A series RLC circuit obeys L d^2q/dt^2 + R dq/dt + q/C = 0. Its free response changes from oscillatory to non-oscillatory at a critical resistance R_c that depends only on L and C.
The only combination of L and C with the SI units of resistance (ohm) is sqrt(L/C), the characteristic impedance of the circuit; the transition to non-oscillatory behaviour occurs when the resistance matches this impedance.
R_c = sqrt(L / C)

A string of length L with fixed ends carries N equally spaced beads of mass m at spacing a = L/(N+1), and the massless string between them is under tension T; the exact normal-mode frequencies are f_n = (1/pi) sqrt(T/(m a)) sin(n pi/(2(N+1))) for n = 1, ..., N.
In the continuum limit N -> infinity at fixed L and fixed mu = m/a, the beaded string becomes a uniform string with wave speed v = sqrt(T/mu), whose modes are f_n = n v/(2L).
For a piano-like string modelled with N = 1000 beads, the highest mode n = N is considered, and N is large enough that the continuum limit applies.
f_N = N v/(2L)

A quantum Brownian particle linearly coupled to an Ohmic bath with friction coefficient gamma experiences a fluctuating force whose symmetrized two-sided spectral density, S_F(omega) = integral_{-infinity}^{infinity} <{F(t), F(0)}/2> exp(i omega t) dt, is S_F(omega) = gamma hbar omega coth( hbar omega / (2 k_B T) ) (quantum fluctuation-dissipation theorem).
In the same two-sided convention, the classical Langevin force with <F(t) F(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t') has the flat spectrum 2 gamma k_B T.
Only frequencies satisfying hbar |omega| << k_B T are relevant to the dynamics considered.
In this regime the quantum spectrum reduces to the classical white-noise spectrum, S_F(omega) = 2 gamma k_B T, with relative corrections of order (hbar omega / k_B T)^2.

In sea water of density rho = 1025 kg/m^3 at rest under g = 9.81 m/s^2, the gauge pressure at depth d is p_g = rho g d; at depths of 20.2 m and 10.1 m this gives p_g = 2.0 atm and 1.0 atm respectively (1 atm = 101325 Pa).
A small air bubble rises slowly from 20.2 m to 10.1 m; the air behaves as an ideal gas and remains at the temperature of the water.
For an isothermal ideal gas Boyle's law holds: p V = constant.
Applying Boyle's law between the two depths, the bubble's volume doubles: V_2 = 2 V_1.

A damped oscillator m x'' + b x' + k x = F0 cos(omega t), with b > 0, has the steady-state solution x = A cos(omega t - delta), where A = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4 beta^2 omega^2), tan(delta) = 2 beta omega / (omega0^2 - omega^2), beta = b/(2m) and omega0^2 = k/m.
The driving frequency is now fixed at the natural frequency, omega = omega0.
The steady-state amplitude reduces to A = F0/(b omega0), and the displacement lags the driving force by exactly a quarter of a period.

A weakly damped oscillator (beta << omega0) has displacement x(t) = A0 e^{-beta t} cos(omega_d t + phi), with omega_d^2 = omega0^2 - beta^2 and omega0^2 = k/m.
Its instantaneous mechanical energy is E = (1/2) m x'^2 + (1/2) k x^2, which fluctuates within each cycle because the damping force does work non-uniformly.
Denote by <E>(t) the energy averaged over one period 2 pi/omega_d of the fast oscillation, treating the slowly varying envelope e^{-beta t} as constant over that period.
To leading order in beta/omega0 the cycle-averaged energy decays exponentially, <E>(t) = (1/2) k A0^2 e^{-2 beta t}.

The free Schroedinger equation i hbar dpsi/dt = -(hbar^2/2m) d^2psi/dx^2 can be written as a diffusion equation dpsi/dt = D_q d^2psi/dx^2 with complex diffusivity D_q = i hbar/(2m), of magnitude hbar/(2m).
For the diffusion equation du/dt = D d^2u/dx^2 the variance of an initially localized packet grows linearly, <x^2>(t) = 2 D t.
A free quantum wave packet therefore spreads diffusively, its position variance growing as <Delta x^2>(t) = hbar t/m.

Any one-dimensional motion satisfying x'' = -omega^2 x, with omega > 0, is periodic: the system returns to the same position and velocity after every interval T = 2 pi/omega.
A mechanical oscillator is observed with a stopwatch to return exactly to its initial position and velocity after every interval of T seconds.
The oscillator's displacement therefore obeys x'' = -(2 pi/T)^2 x.

In a homogeneous half-space y > 0 the temperature obeys dT/dt = alpha d^2T/dy^2 with constant thermal diffusivity alpha.
For real wavenumber k, the equation admits solutions exp(i k y - i omega t) with complex frequency fixed by the dispersion relation omega = -i alpha k^2, i.e. pure exponential decay in time.
The surface temperature is driven periodically, T(0, t) = T_0 + Delta T cos(omega t) with real omega > 0, and the temperature must remain bounded as y -> infinity.
Solving the same dispersion relation for complex k at real omega and keeping the branch that is bounded at large y, the temperature oscillation decays into the solid as exp(-y / delta) with penetration depth delta = sqrt(2 alpha / omega).

A Brownian particle of mass m obeys m dv/dt = -gamma v + xi(t), where gamma = 6 pi eta a is the Stokes friction coefficient and <xi(t) xi(t')> = 2 gamma k_B T delta(t - t').
The velocity is an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process whose autocorrelation decays exponentially, <v(0) v(t)> = <v^2> exp(-gamma t), with <v^2> = k_B T/m by equipartition.
The Green-Kubo formula gives the diffusion coefficient as D = integral_0^infinity <v(0) v(t)> dt.
Evaluating the integral gives D = k_B T/(m gamma).

A scalar field phi(x,t) obeys the one-dimensional Klein-Gordon equation (1/c^2) d^2phi/dt^2 - d^2phi/dx^2 + (m c/hbar)^2 phi = 0, with c the speed of light, m > 0 a constant mass and hbar the reduced Planck constant.
Plane-wave solutions phi = exp(i(kx - omega t)) with real k are substituted, giving omega^2 = c^2 k^2 + (m c^2/hbar)^2.
The phase velocity is defined as v_p = omega/k and the group velocity as v_g = d omega/dk, with k > 0 and the positive root omega > 0 taken.
v_p v_g = c^2

A passive solute of molecular diffusivity D is carried by steady Poiseuille flow in a straight circular tube of radius a, with axial velocity u(r) = 2 U (1 - r^2/a^2), where U is the cross-sectional mean speed.
The concentration c(r, z, t) obeys the advection-diffusion equation dc/dt + u(r) dc/dz = D (nabla_perp^2 c + d^2c/dz^2) with zero flux through the tube wall (partial derivatives understood).
The solute cloud is observed at times t >> a^2 / D, so that radial diffusion has mixed the solute across the section, and its axial extent is much larger than a.
The cross-sectionally averaged concentration obeys a one-dimensional advection-diffusion equation in the frame moving with speed U, with effective axial diffusivity D_eff = D + a^2 U^2 / (48 D).

A mass m on a spring of constant k moves along a line under a viscous drag force -b dx/dt, so that m d^2x/dt^2 + b dx/dt + k x = 0 with b, k, m > 0 in SI units.
The damping is subcritical, b^2 < 4 m k. Write gamma = b/(2m) and omega_d = sqrt(k/m - gamma^2).
x_n denotes the value of x at its n-th successive local maximum, n = 1, 2, 3, ...
ln(x_n / x_(n+1)) = 2 pi gamma / omega_d

For the driven oscillator x'' + 2 beta x' + omega0^2 x = (F0/m) cos(omega t), the steady-state amplitude is A(omega) = (F0/m) / sqrt((omega0^2 - omega^2)^2 + 4 beta^2 omega^2).
The exact maximum of A over omega occurs at omega_r^2 = omega0^2 - 2 beta^2 and equals A_max = (F0/m) / (2 beta sqrt(omega0^2 - beta^2)).
The oscillator is lightly damped: beta << omega0.
In this regime the peak amplitude is A_max = F0/(2 m beta omega0), with a relative error of order beta^2/omega0^2.

An incompressible fluid at rest under uniform gravity g has a smooth density profile rho(z) that decreases with height z, and its pressure obeys dp/dz = -rho(z) g.
A small rigid body of volume V has density rho_b equal to the fluid density rho_0 at its equilibrium height; its size is much smaller than the length rho/|drho/dz|, so the fluid it displaces has the density evaluated at the height of its centre.
Archimedes' principle holds in the stratified fluid (the fluid exerts an upward force equal to g times the mass of the displaced fluid); viscous drag and added mass are neglected, and displacements are small enough that drho/dz may be treated as constant.
The body oscillates harmonically about its equilibrium height with angular frequency N given by N^2 = -(g/rho_0) drho/dz, evaluated at the equilibrium height.

A capacitor C charged to q0 is connected at t = 0 through a switch to a series combination of an inductor L and resistor R, with R small enough that the discharge is oscillatory at angular frequency omega_d.
The product RC has the dimensions of time and is the characteristic time constant associated with a resistor and capacitor in a circuit.
The oscillating charge is confined within an exponentially decaying envelope whose time constant is fixed by the dissipative element R together with the energy-storing elements.
The charge on the capacitor is q(t) = q0 e^{-t/(RC)} cos(omega_d t).

An incompressible liquid of density rho rotates rigidly about the vertical z axis with angular velocity Omega under uniform gravity g directed along -z; in the co-rotating frame the liquid is at rest and satisfies grad p = rho (-g e_z + Omega^2 r e_r), where r is the distance from the axis.
The solution with pressure p_a at the point r = 0, z = z_0 is p(r, z) = p_a + (1/2) rho Omega^2 r^2 - rho g (z - z_0), which is a polynomial in the parameter Omega^2.
The parameter Omega is continued to the imaginary value i omega with omega real, so that Omega^2 becomes -omega^2.
p(r, z) = p_a - (1/2) rho omega^2 r^2 - rho g (z - z_0), which is the hydrostatic pressure field of a liquid at rest in an inertial frame under gravity together with an inward radial body force of magnitude omega^2 r per unit mass, as inside a uniformly dense self-gravitating cylinder with omega^2 equal to 2 pi G rho

A uniform string of length L and wave speed c whose displacement vanishes at both ends, u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0, has normal modes sin(n pi x/L) cos(omega_n t) with omega_n = n pi c/L for n = 1, 2, 3, ...
A second string of the same length and wave speed is observed to vibrate freely with a discrete spectrum of normal-mode frequencies omega_n = n pi c/L, n = 1, 2, 3, ...
The spectrum of a uniform string is determined by its boundary conditions.
The second string must therefore have its displacement clamped at the ends, u(x_end, t) = 0 at both x_end values, so its boundary conditions are the same as those of the first string.
